findings.title: F-2025-9438 Incorrect Pool Deserialization Causing Program Failure
findings.description:
The program attempts to deserialize a Raydium Concentrated Liquidity pool state using a data structure intended for Raydium CPMM pools. This causes a type confusion during deserialization, leading to a size mismatch and resulting in a runtime panic at `from_bytes>SizeMismatch`. 
The root cause is the incorrect use of the `PoolState` and `PoolState2` types for different pool programs without accounting for their differing memory layouts.
An attacker could trigger this error by invoking the affected function with a Concentrated Liquidity pool account, causing the program to halt execution.
The impact is critical: the program becomes entirely unusable whenever this deserialization error occurs, leading to a denial of service.

findings.title: F-2025-9391 Missing Nonce Allows Repeated Executions of the Same Signed Generation Request
findings.description:
The `generate_handler` function verifies a signed message from an off-chain verifier but does not include a nonce or unique identifier in the signed message payload. 
This allows an attacker or user to replay the same signed message multiple times before the deadline expires, leading to repeated execution of the generation request.
The root cause is the absence of replay protection such as a one-time-use nonce or incrementing counter in the message hashing logic.
While the financial impact is unclear due to ambiguous design intent, repeated executions could lead to unintended state changes or resource consumption.
The impact is considered low due to the lack of clear exploitability for direct fund loss, but it remains a security concern depending on the intended usage model.

findings.title: F-2025-9390 WSOL Price Derived Solely from Raydium Pool May Be Manipulable
findings.description:
The protocol derives the USD value of WSOL by querying the WSOL/USDT price from a Raydium DEX pool without using an oracle or price validation mechanism. 
This exposes the system to potential price manipulation through flash loans, sandwich attacks, or low-liquidity exploitation, especially during periods of high volatility or low trading volume.
The root cause is the direct reliance on a single on-chain DEX pool without safeguards such as time-weighted average prices (TWAP) or deviation checks.
An attacker could manipulate the pool price temporarily to influence off-chain processes that depend on this rate.
The impact is low but non-negligible, as manipulated prices could lead to incorrect financial calculations or unfair advantages in protocol operations.
